title: The Ash'ari school
hook: paper and ink, and the speech they carry: the Ash'ari middle way

segments.voice: Yesterday, Imam al-Ash'ari, and your line: reason for tradition. Did you find a good reason for something you inherited? Today, what grew from him. Day one thousand two hundred forty-five.

A printed Qur'an, open on a reading stand. Paper from a mill. Ink from a factory. Glue in the spine, a cover someone designed. Every bit of it was made, at a certain time, by certain hands. Now someone opens it and recites, and the voice is made too: breath, throat, a person who was born on a certain day. So here's the question from the trial, asked again with the book in your hands. Is the Qur'an created? Ahmad ibn Hanbal said no, and would not say otherwise. The Mu'tazilah said yes. The school that grew from al-Ash'ari gave an answer with a line drawn through the middle. Today, that line.
screen: `PAPER, INK, A VOICE.` → `ALL OF IT MADE.` → `SO IS THE QUR'AN CREATED?`

segments.voice: The Ash'ari answer goes like this. Allah's speech is one of His attributes, and like Him it's eternal. It isn't a made thing. But the copy in your hands, the ink and the paper, the sounds in your mouth when you recite, the memory of it in a child's head: all of that is created. So when you hold a printed Qur'an, you're holding something made that carries something unmade. The recitation is yours. The speech is His. That's the key idea, and it shows the school's whole style. Take a fight with two sides, and find where each side is right. With the Mu'tazilah, the Ash'aris agree that reason matters and that the things of this world are created. With the people of hadith, they agree that the Qur'an is Allah's speech and not a creature. They're called a middle way, between reason running ahead of revelation and a refusal to reason at all. Over the centuries the school drew names that are still taught. Al-Baqillani argued for it. Al-Juwayni taught it. His student al-Ghazali, whose books are still read, wrote within it. It became tied especially with scholars of the Shafi'i and Maliki schools of law. Not everyone accepted it. Hanbali scholars, as we'll see in a couple of days, often kept their distance, and Shia theology took its own road. But the Ash'ari move is the one to keep: the ink is made, and the speech it carries is not.
screen: `HIS SPEECH IS ETERNAL.` · `THE INK AND THE VOICE ARE MADE.` · `AGREE WITH EACH SIDE WHERE IT'S RIGHT.` · then, large: `A MIDDLE WAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn its key idea by feeling it. Settle, and breathe. If there's a Qur'an or any well-loved book nearby, rest a hand on it. If not, rest a hand on your chest. Notice the made things: the paper, the cover, your own breath and voice. Then notice what they carry: words and meaning that didn't start with the paper. Say quietly the line from the Ash'ari answer: the recitation is mine, the speech is His. If you'd rather, just hold the thought: made things can carry what isn't made. The bell holds the time.
The Ash'ari school. The theology that grew from al-Ash'ari: reason in service of revelation, and a middle way on the created Qur'an. Today's word.
Your line: the middle way. Today, when you hear two sides arguing, find one thing each side gets right. Tomorrow, Imam al-Maturidi. Day one thousand two hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: The Ash'ari school is taught in Sunni seminaries as a school of theology, and Ash'aris hold that Allah's speech is eternal while the written copies and recitations of the Qur'an are created.

trapdoor: what you thought: one man's personal opinions about God.
what it means: a school of Sunni theology that uses reason to defend revelation, often called a middle way.
what a scholar hears: Allah's eternal speech distinguished from the created letters, ink and sounds that express it.
